190.title: Seven baskets (Mark 8:1–10)
190.hook: a second feeding, in Gentile country, four thousand fed
190.howItsDone: Many churches call communion the Eucharist, from the Greek word for giving thanks, and many Christians volunteer at food banks and shared meals that feed people beyond their own congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sigh toward heaven and one Aramaic word, ephphatha. Your line was a sound you usually ignore. What sound did you finally hear? Day one hundred ninety.

Have you ever had déjà vu so strong you almost laughed? That's today. A huge crowd, out in the middle of nowhere. Nothing to eat. Jesus turns to the disciples and says, I feel for these people. And the disciples, who watched five thousand fed from five loaves just two chapters ago, ask where anyone could find bread out here. You want to shake them. But before we're too hard on them, it's worth asking how often we forget what already happened to us. Today: seven baskets.
screen: `A HUGE CROWD, AGAIN.` → `NOTHING TO EAT, AGAIN.` → `WHERE COULD WE FIND BREAD?`

segments.voice: This time Jesus speaks first, in the old King James Bible: "I have compassion on the multitude, because they have now been with me three days, and have nothing to eat." Three days. They've stayed so long their food ran out. And some, he says, came from far away; send them home hungry and they'll collapse on the road. The disciples answer: "From whence can a man satisfy these men with bread here in the wilderness?" He asks the same question as before. What have you got? Seven loaves. A few small fish. He has everyone sit on the ground, gives thanks, breaks, and hands it to the disciples to give out. The Greek for gave thanks is the word that gives us eucharist, the name many churches use for communion. Four thousand eat and are satisfied, and seven baskets are left over. So why tell a second feeding at all? Look at where we are. Yesterday Jesus was in the ten cities, Gentile country. Many readers think this crowd is mostly Gentile, the same people the Syrophoenician mother spoke for. The first time, twelve baskets, like the twelve tribes of Israel. This time, seven, a number of fullness and completeness, and some hear the nations in it. The crumbs she asked for became a meal with leftovers. Even the baskets are different. The first feeding used a Greek word for a small wicker basket. This one uses a word for a big one, large enough, in Acts, to lower Paul over a city wall. Then they sail off to a place called Dalmanutha. Nobody today knows where that was.
screen: `THREE DAYS, AND NOTHING TO EAT.` · `HE GAVE THANKS — EUCHARIST.` · `TWELVE BASKETS, THEN SEVEN.` · `DALMANUTHA: NOBODY KNOWS WHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed someone outside your circle. Settle, and breathe. Picture the people you feed without thinking: family, friends, the office birthday. Now look just past the edge of that circle. A neighbor you don't know. A coworker from another team. A stranger at a shelter or a food bank. Someone who's been waiting a while, and came from far. Choose one way you could feed someone outside your circle this week. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you have, the way he did before he broke the bread. The bell holds the time.
Seven baskets. The leftovers from a second feeding, four thousand, in Gentile country, enough again.
Your line: enough again. Today, feed someone outside your usual circle, and trust there'll be enough. Day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Hard hearts in a boat (Mark 8:11–21)
191.hook: they've forgotten bread and worry, after two feedings
191.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a habit of remembering God's help in the past, through gratitude journals, testimonies or prayers of thanksgiving, as a way of meeting present worries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seven baskets: four thousand fed in Gentile country. Your line was enough again. Who outside your circle did you feed? Day one hundred ninety-one.

One loaf. That's the whole inventory. A few verses back, seven baskets of leftovers. Now the disciples are back in the boat, crossing the lake again, somebody checks the bag, and Mark says they had forgotten to take bread: there's one loaf with them, and that's all. It's the wallet-left-on-the-counter moment, out on the water. And while they mutter about lunch, Jesus is trying to tell them something else entirely. They miss it. Mark doesn't tidy the scene up for them. Today: hard hearts in a boat.
screen: `ONE LOAF IN THE BOAT.` → `THE BREAD THEY FORGOT.` → `THEY MISS WHAT HE SAYS.`

segments.voice: Just before they sailed, some Pharisees had asked Jesus for a sign from heaven, proof on demand. He sighed deeply and refused: no sign will be given to this generation. Now in the boat he warns, in the old King James Bible: "Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod." Leaven, you might remember from day twenty-four, is the bit of old dough that works invisibly through a whole batch. Mark doesn't define it here. Some readers take it as an attitude that spreads: demanding proof, playing power games. And the disciples say to each other, he's talking about bread because we forgot to bring any. So he asks them a string of questions, and they come fast: "perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?" Then a quiz. When I broke five loaves for five thousand, how many baskets of leftovers? Twelve, they say. And the seven for four thousand? Seven. And he says, "How is it that ye do not understand?" That's where Mark leaves it. No answer. They've watched thousands fed, twice, and they're worried about lunch with him sitting right there. And notice the one loaf in the boat. Some readers hear a quiet hint: they're not as short of bread as they think, because the one who fed the crowds is on board. Mark ends there, mid-crossing, with two counts of baskets and one loaf in the bag.
screen: `NO SIGN FOR THIS GENERATION.` · `BEWARE THE LEAVEN.` · `TWELVE BASKETS, THEN SEVEN.` · `ONE LOAF, AND HE'S ON BOARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember one time you had enough. Settle, and breathe. Go back to a time you were sure you wouldn't make it. Money was short, or time, or strength, or hope. And somehow there was enough. Someone showed up. A door opened. You got through. Stay with that memory. Count the baskets, so to speak: what was left over afterward? Now hold it next to whatever you're worried about today. If you pray, you can give thanks for that time. The bell holds the time.
Leaven, the old dough that works invisibly through a whole batch, Jesus's warning about an attitude that spreads, right before a quiz about two feedings.
Your line: do you not yet understand? Today, when a worry comes, remember one time there was enough, before you panic. Day one hundred ninety-one.

192.title: Men like trees (Mark 8:22–26)
192.hook: the only two-stage healing: first blurry, then clear
192.howItsDone: Some Christians describe faith as a journey rather than a single moment, and some churches pray for healing more than once, taking comfort from the second touch in this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hard hearts in a boat: the leaven warning, one loaf, two feedings forgotten, and a string of questions. Your line was do you not yet understand? What did you remember? Day one hundred ninety-two.

If you've ever worn glasses, you know the moment at the eye doctor. They click through the lenses. Better like this? Or like this? The chart goes from smudge, to almost, to sharp. Today's healing happens a lot like that. At Bethsaida, people bring a blind man to Jesus, and Mark tells it in two stages, with a pause in the middle. He even tells us what the man saw halfway through. Today: men like trees.

Jesus takes the man by the hand and leads him out of the village. Picture that walk: a blind man holding a stranger's hand down a dirt road. Then Jesus spits on his eyes, lays his hands on him, and asks, do you see anything? In the old King James Bible, the man looks up and says, "I see men as trees, walking." Blurry shapes, tall and moving. He can tell they're people only because trees don't walk. It's an honest answer. He doesn't pretend. So Jesus lays his hands on his eyes a second time, "and he was restored, and saw every man clearly." Clearly, and far: lexicons give Mark's Greek word as plainly, even at a distance. Why would Mark tell a healing in two stages? He doesn't say. But look where he puts it. Just before, Jesus asked the disciples, having eyes, see ye not? Tomorrow, Peter will say who Jesus is, and then, in the very next breath, prove he only half understands it. Some readers think this blind man is a picture of the disciples. They see something. It's blurry. People look like trees. They'll need a second touch. Read that way, the story makes room for an honest halfway: the right answer to do you see? can be, sort of. And in Mark, sort of isn't where it ends. There's a second touch.
screen: `LED BY THE HAND OUT OF TOWN.` · `I SEE MEN AS TREES, WALKING.` · `A SECOND TOUCH, THEN CLEARLY.` · `A PICTURE OF THE DISCIPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with a slow change. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in you that's changing slowly. A habit you're breaking. A grief that's easing. A faith, or a doubt, that's taking shape. Ask it honestly, like Jesus asked the man: do you see anything yet? Maybe the answer is, sort of. Blurry. Men like trees. Let that be all right. If you pray, you can ask for the second touch. If not, just thank yourself for getting halfway. The bell holds the time.
Clearly, the word for what the blind man finally saw, after a first touch left him seeing only men like trees, walking.
Your line: sight comes in stages. Today, be as patient with one slow change, in you or in someone else, as Jesus was with that man's eyes. Day one hundred ninety-two.

193.title: You are the Christ (Mark 8:27–30)
193.hook: at Caesarea Philippi, Peter says it: you are the Messiah, the anointed one
193.carry: who do you say I am?
193.howItsDone: Christians confess Jesus as the Christ, and in churches that use the Creeds, the congregation says it aloud in worship; some Christians use Peter's question as a regular prompt for personal prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a blind man at Bethsaida saw men like trees, walking, and only then saw clearly. Your line was sight comes in stages. Did something come a little clearer? Day one hundred ninety-three.

Someone new starts at work, and before anyone really knows them, the theories begin. He's the one who used to be at that other place. She's like the last manager, only quieter. Now Mark takes us north, to the towns of Caesarea Philippi. Jesus and his friends are walking, and on the road he asks a simple question: "Whom do men say that I am?" They have the talk ready. Some say John the Baptist. Some say Elijah. Some say one of the prophets. Then he turns the question around, and there's nowhere to hide: "But whom say ye that I am?" And Peter answers.
screen: `A ROAD FAR IN THE NORTH.` → `WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?` → `BUT WHOM SAY YE?`

segments.voice: Peter says four words in the old King James Bible: "Thou art the Christ." Start with the word itself. Christ is not Jesus's last name. There was no Mr. and Mrs. Christ. It's a title. The Greek word is Christos, and it means the anointed one. It translates a Hebrew word, mashiach, which comes into English as Messiah. Anointed means oil poured on your head. In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Samuel pours oil on young David to mark him as king, and priests were anointed too. In Jesus's day there were Jews who hoped for an anointed one, a king from David's family. When Peter says Christ, he's saying: you are that one. Notice where this sits. Back in the storm on the lake, the disciples asked, what manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? Now someone finally says it out loud. Mark's very first line had already told the reader: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The disciples just took half the book to catch up. And then the strange part: Jesus charges them to tell no one. Scholars still argue about why, and Mark never fully explains. One hint comes in the very next scene: the word Christ meant something different to Peter than it would turn out to mean. Christians confess it in their creeds: Jesus is the Christ. But notice how he asked. Not what do people say. What do you say.
screen: `WHOM SAY YE THAT I AM?` · `CHRIST IS A TITLE, NOT A SURNAME.` · `ANOINTED: OIL ON A KING'S HEAD.` · `HIS ORDER: TELL NO ONE.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the question be asked of you. Settle, and breathe slowly. Maybe you pray to Jesus every day. Maybe you're learning about him for someone you love. Maybe you honestly don't know. Imagine the road, the walking, and the question turned toward you: who do you say I am? Don't reach for the right answer, or the answer your family gives. Find your own word, even if it's teacher, or stranger, or I'm not sure yet. If you pray, you can simply say what you find. Just be honest. The bell holds the time.
Christ. From the Greek Christos, the anointed one, the same word as the Hebrew Messiah. A title, not a surname.
Your line: who do you say I am? Today, notice one time you repeat what others say about someone, and ask what you'd say yourself. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Take up your cross (Mark 8:31–38)
194.hook: Peter rebukes him about suffering, is called Satan, and hears: lose your life to save it
194.howItsDone: Some Christians speak of their own small sacrifices as carrying the cross, and some take on a daily act of self-giving; in Lent especially, churches that keep the season invite people to give something up for the sake of others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the road near Caesarea Philippi, Peter called him the Christ, the anointed one. Your line was who do you say I am? What did you find when you asked it? Day one hundred ninety-four.

Thou art the Christ. Peter has just said it, out loud, in front of everyone. Top of the class. And then, straight away, Jesus starts to explain what that will mean, and none of it is what they hoped to hear. He'll suffer many things. He'll be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes. He'll be killed. And after three days he'll rise again. Mark adds that he said it openly, no riddles this time. So Peter does what any loyal friend might do. He takes Jesus aside, quietly, and tells him off. No. Not that. Not you. And Jesus turns around, looks at the others, and answers Peter in front of all of them.
screen: `TOP OF THE CLASS.` → `HE MUST SUFFER.` → `PETER TAKES HIM ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the answer, in the old King James Bible: "Get thee behind me, Satan." From top of the class to Satan in a handful of verses. It sounds brutal, but listen to the word. In Hebrew, satan means an adversary, the one who stands in your way. One way to hear it: Peter has put himself on the road, in front of Jesus, blocking it. Get behind me: go back to following. Then Jesus calls the whole crowd over, with his disciples, and says: "Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." Today a cross can be a necklace or a steeple. To that crowd it was nothing of the kind. It was a Roman way of putting people to death, in public, and as Mark will later show, a cross was carried through the streets to the place of death. The words may well have made them flinch. And then the riddle at the center: "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it." Grip your life too tightly and it slips away. Spend it on something bigger and you find it. Christians have read this in more than one way. For the early church, under persecution, it could mean dying for the faith. Luke's version adds the word daily, and some hear it as ordinary, everyday self-giving: the parent up at 3am, the friend who shows up. And some churches today say plainly what it does not mean: it is not a command to stay in harm or abuse. The verse itself holds both halves, side by side: lose, and save.
screen: `FROM TOP OF THE CLASS TO SATAN.` · `SATAN: THE ONE IN THE WAY.` · `A CROSS WAS AN EXECUTION.` · `LOSE IT TO FIND IT.` · then, large: `TAKE UP HIS CROSS, AND FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one small thing to give up for someone today. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person. What would make their day lighter? Maybe it's your turn to choose the show, or the last slice, or twenty minutes you'd planned for yourself. Something that costs a little, not a lot. Picture yourself handing it over. Notice whether your hands want to hold on. If you pray, you can offer it to God as part of following. If you don't, just decide. The bell holds the time.
Cross, in Jesus's day the walk of the condemned; in the life of faith, what it costs to follow him, deny yourself, and go.
Your line: lose it to find it. Today, give the thing away, and watch whether you feel smaller or larger afterward. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: Listen to him (Mark 9:1–13)
195.hook: the transfiguration, and the one instruction from the cloud: listen to him
195.carry: let it change what you do
195.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate the Transfiguration as a feast, on August 6 in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican calendars, and many Protestant churches read the story on the Sunday before Lent; Christians often speak of listening to Jesus through reading the Gospels and in silent prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter stood in the road and heard take up your cross. Your line was lose it to find it. What did you give away, and how did it feel? Day one hundred ninety-five.

Six days later, Mark says, Jesus takes three friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain, just the four of them. And up there, he changes in front of them. His clothes turn shining, dazzling white, and Mark, who loves a homely detail, says they were whiter than any laundryman on earth could get them. Then two figures appear beside him, talking with him: Elijah and Moses, great prophets from centuries before. And Peter, bless him, has to say something. It's good for us to be here! Let's build three shelters: one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. And Mark adds, gently: "For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid." He didn't know what to say, so he said something. We have all been Peter.
screen: `A HIGH MOUNTAIN, JUST FOUR.` → `WHITER THAN ANY LAUNDRY.` → `LET'S BUILD THREE SHELTERS.`

segments.voice: While Peter is still planning construction, a cloud comes down and covers them, and a voice speaks out of it. In the King James Bible: "This is my beloved Son: hear him." That's it. One sentence of introduction, one instruction. Not build. Not explain. Hear him. The Greek word means listen, and in the Bible listening is never just sound in the ears. In Hebrew, the same word covers hearing and obeying. To really listen is to let it change what you do. Notice what the voice doesn't say. It doesn't say listen to Moses and Elijah too. Many Christians read those two as standing for the Law and the Prophets, the whole Hebrew Bible, gathered around Jesus. And then, suddenly, they look around and see no one any more, only Jesus, with them. The cloud is gone. The glow is gone. What's left is an ordinary man on a mountain, and the instruction to listen to him. Mark never names the mountain. Christian tradition since early centuries has pointed to Mount Tabor in Galilee, and others suggest Mount Hermon, much nearer Caesarea Philippi. The text is silent. On the way down he tells them to tell no one until he has risen from the dead, and they puzzle over what rising from the dead could mean. Christians call this the transfiguration, from the Latin for being changed in form. Orthodox Christians hold it especially dear, and Catholic, Anglican and many other churches keep it as a feast on the sixth of August.
screen: `A CLOUD, AND ONE SENTENCE.` · `LISTEN MEANS HEAR AND DO.` · `NO ONE LEFT BUT JESUS.` · `A MOUNTAIN MARK NEVER NAMES.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON: HEAR HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be the one who listens. Settle, and breathe. For the next two minutes, don't plan anything, don't fix anything, don't build any shelters. Just listen. First the sounds of the room. Then the sounds beyond it, far away. Then the quiet underneath. If you pray, you can hold the line hear him, and wait, without filling the silence. If a thought wants to talk, let it pass like a cloud. The bell holds the time.
Transfiguration, from Latin for being changed in form: the mountain where Jesus shone before Peter, James and John, and a voice said, listen.
Your line: let it change what you do. Today, in one conversation, listen more than you speak. When you feel the urge to build three shelters, wait. Day one hundred ninety-five.

196.title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
196.hook: a desperate father: I believe; help my unbelief
196.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the father's words, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," as a short prayer in times of doubt, and some pastors point to this story to say that faith and doubt can live together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the mountain, a voice from the cloud gave one instruction. Your line was let it change what you do. Did you manage to listen more than you spoke? Day one hundred ninety-six. The end of another week.

From the shining mountain straight down into a mess. At the bottom there's a crowd, and an argument. The disciples who stayed behind have tried to heal a boy, and they couldn't. The boy's father pushes through. His son, he says, has a spirit that takes his speech, throws him to the ground, makes him foam and grind his teeth and go rigid. Since he was a child. It has thrown him into fire and into water. Years of nights like that, and now even the disciples have failed. So when he gets to Jesus, his hope is worn thin. In the King James Bible he says: "if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us." If.
screen: `DOWN FROM THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THE DISCIPLES COULDN'T.` → `IF THOU CANST DO ANY THING.`

segments.voice: Jesus catches the word and hands the if back. In the King James text: "If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth." And the father cries out, with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once. I believe, and I don't. I trust you, and I'm terrified. He doesn't pretend. And Jesus doesn't send him away to come back when his faith is tidier. He heals the boy, and lifts him by the hand. In Mark's telling, half a faith, handed over honestly, is where it starts. The Greek word for unbelief is apistia, faith with a no in front of it. Some Christians call this verse a lifeline, because it puts doubt and faith in the same heart, in the same sentence. Readers today often notice that the boy's signs sound like epilepsy. Mark describes a spirit, and Christians understand stories like this in different ways; the text simply tells it as a spirit. Later, the disciples ask privately why they failed. His answer, in the King James: "This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting." Now look back at the week. Seven baskets: enough again. Hard hearts in a boat: do you not yet understand? A blind man seeing men like trees. Peter: you are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. And now this father. Again and again this week, someone sees in part, and is helped further along.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold both halves honestly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you trust, and one thing you doubt. About God, about yourself, about someone you love. Don't solve either one. Just let them sit side by side. If you pray, you can say the father's words, slowly, as many times as you like: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If you don't pray, you can simply say: some of me trusts, some of me doesn't, and that's where I am. The bell holds the time.
Apistia, faith with a no in front of it: a father's cry holding belief and doubt in the same breath, and it was enough.
Your line: bring the half you have. Today, when you feel only half sure, don't wait to be certain. That's enough to bring. Day one hundred ninety-six.
